hints: Look carefully at the phrase 'mitotic cell cycle', not just 'mitosis'. Does it mean only nuclear division, or the whole cycle from one cell to two cells?
Remember the cell cycle = interphase + mitosis (which includes telophase) + cytokinesis. Check if each of 1, 2 and 3 fits into that bigger picture.
walkthrough:
**Recall what the mitotic cell cycle means**

Think of it as the full story of how one parent cell makes two identical daughter cells. It is much bigger than just mitosis alone.

It includes: interphase (growth and DNA replication) + mitosis (nuclear division) + cytokinesis (splitting the cytoplasm).

**Check each event in the list**

1 interphase: Yes, this is the longest part where the cell grows and copies its DNA ready for division.

2 telophase: Yes, this is the last stage of mitosis itself, when two new nuclei reform. Since mitosis is part of the cycle, telophase is too.

3 cytokinesis: Yes, this is the final splitting of cytoplasm to make two separate cells, and it completes the cycle.

**Put it together**

All three events belong in the mitotic cell cycle. That gives us 1, 2 and 3, which is option A.

options.A: Correct and reassuring. Interphase, telophase (as part of mitosis) and cytokinesis are all essential parts of the complete mitotic cell cycle.
options.B: Leaves out cytokinesis, but cytokinesis is needed to divide the cytoplasm and actually form two daughter cells.
options.C: Leaves out telophase, but telophase is the final stage of mitosis when the two daughter nuclei form.
options.D: Leaves out interphase, but interphase is the vital first stage where DNA is replicated before any division can happen.
